And as soon as his word was accepted,
he began to magnify himself in his soul,
and he went to the camp,
and cast an accusation against Tāj al-Dīn bar Mukhtaṣ, saying
that, behold, he had gathered forty myriad [pieces of] gold for himself.
Now the Jew, who was the Sahib-Diwan,
when he heard his words, became boastful,
and said in his heart:
"If this is proven against this man,
how much more, then, will be proven against his brother, who is the associate of Tāj al-Dīn?"
For he ruled over the regions even more than he did,
and his hand was extended more in taking and giving.
Therefore he began to entice Faraj Allāh,
and showed him
that by this action
not only would Tāj al-Dīn be harmed [by it?], but also his brother would be injured even more.
Now when the wretched Faraj Allāh saw
that he was not able to resist his command,
nor to stand against him,
and that if he retracted his word,
the Emirs of the camp would condemn him and kill him,
some people said to him:
"Write in your own handwriting
that you spoke what you spoke in drunkenness,
and that these two persons—
namely Tāj al-Dīn and his associate—did not {OCR?} wrong anyone, nor take anything unjustly,
and give [it] {OCR?} to the Sahib-Diwan,
and he will immediately manage your affair and save you;
moreover, he will make you an associate and colleague of these [men]."
So he simply accepted this,
and wrote with his own hand concerning these things,
and gave [it] to the Sahib-Diwan.
Now the deceitful Jew, as soon as the paper fell into his hands,
took it and went in to the King of Kings [and said]:
"What do you command concerning a man who yesterday spoke that story,
and today wrote handwriting like this?" And he replied:
"Truly, a man such as this deserves death."
And at that very hour they killed him there.
And he further pointed out that he had associates in Mosul,
two who were worse than he.
And he commanded that these also should be killed;
and he sent {OCR?} in haste to Mosul for Mu'ayyad bar Mu'ayyad the scribe,
and for Amīn al-Dīn bar Muḥtasib the Arbelaean.
And after some days Emir Matthew was sent—
an active man and a great pillar of the Christians in the region of Mosul—
from the camp to the city of Siirt,
to collect the tribute from them according to the custom of the Mongols.
